questions.stem: A 54 year old woman has just had an upper GI endoscopy under intravenous midazolam sedation. In recovery she stops responding to voice. There is no chest movement and no breath sounds for 10 seconds. A carotid pulse is clearly felt at 64 bpm. Her oxygen saturation is 82% and falling.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Unresponsive and not breathing with a pulse present is respiratory arrest; sedatives such as midazolam are a classic cause. No pulse would make it cardiac arrest.

steps.x: This asks what is going on. Name the condition or finding from the stem before looking at the options.
Apnoeic and unresponsive, but **pulse present**, after a sedative.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Not breathing, pulse still there: **respiratory arrest**.

elim: Cardiac arrest has no pulse; her carotid pulse is present.
Can cause reduced consciousness but not apnoea straight after sedation.
There is no seizure activity.
Gives brief loss of consciousness with breathing maintained and rapid recovery.

steps.x: **C. Respiratory arrest.** No breathing + pulse = respiratory arrest; no pulse = cardiac arrest.

questions.stem: A 38 year old man is found apnoeic at home after taking heroin. Paramedics find a carotid pulse of 48 bpm. They cannot open his airway because his jaw is clenched, and no ventilation is given for several minutes. His oxygen saturation is unrecordable and he is deeply cyanosed.
questions.q: Which finding is most likely to show he has progressed to cardiac arrest?
questions.e: Untreated respiratory arrest causes worsening hypoxaemia and hypercapnia, then bradycardia and cardiac arrest. The defining change is loss of the pulse.

steps.x: This asks what is going on. Name the condition or finding from the stem before looking at the options.

clues: no ventilation is given for several minutes
steps.x: Respiratory arrest with a slowing pulse and no ventilation: heading for **cardiac arrest**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Cardiac arrest is defined by **no pulse**.

elim: Can follow hypoxic brain injury but does not define cardiac arrest.
Severe hypoxaemia occurs in respiratory arrest with a pulse still present.
He is already apnoeic; that is respiratory arrest.
Reflects hypoxaemia, not loss of circulation.

steps.x: **B. Loss of the central pulse.** Respiratory arrest becomes cardiac arrest when the pulse is lost.

questions.stem: A 26 year old man is found unresponsive in a hostel bathroom with a syringe beside him. His respiratory rate is 3 breaths per minute, pulse rate 58 bpm, BP 100/62 mmHg and oxygen saturation 76% breathing air. His capillary glucose is 6.1 mmol/L. There are needle track marks on both forearms.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on examination of his eyes?
questions.e: Opioid overdose causes slow or absent breathing with pinpoint pupils; it is the classic specific cause of respiratory arrest.

steps.x: This asks what is going on. Name the condition or finding from the stem before looking at the options.

clues: respiratory rate is 3 breaths per minute
steps.x: Injecting drug use + near apnoea + normal glucose = **opioid overdose**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Opioids constrict the pupils: **bilateral pinpoint pupils**.

elim: Seen with stimulants, anticholinergics or after hypoxic brain injury.
Seen with alcohol, phenytoin or cerebellar lesions.
A sign of raised intracranial pressure developing over time.
Suggests third nerve compression from raised ICP.

steps.x: **B. Bilateral pinpoint pupils.** Opioid overdose = pinpoint pupils + slow or absent breathing.

questions.stem: A 60 year old man is intubated in the Emergency Department after a respiratory arrest. The tube was difficult to place. Two minutes later his oxygen saturation has fallen from 94% to 80% despite bagging with 100% oxygen. His pulse rate is 118 bpm and BP 136/84 mmHg. The doctor examines his chest and abdomen.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on examination?
o: Absent breath sounds at both bases with a distended abdomen
Absent breath sounds on the left only
Stony dullness at the right base
questions.e: After a difficult intubation, falling saturations with absent air entry at both bases and a distending abdomen mean the tube is in the oesophagus, inflating the stomach.

steps.x: This asks what is going on. Name the condition or finding from the stem before looking at the options.
Sats fall right after a difficult intubation = **oesophageal intubation** until proven otherwise.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Gas goes to the stomach, not the lungs: **absent breath sounds at both bases, distended abdomen**.

elim: Suggests the tube has gone too far, into the right main bronchus.
Suggests bronchospasm.
Suggests tension pneumothorax, with hypotension.
Suggests a pleural effusion.

steps.x: **A. Absent breath sounds at both bases with a distended abdomen.** Oesophageal intubation: low SpO2, no air entry at both bases, distended abdomen.

questions.stem: A 47 year old woman is found unresponsive at home beside empty packets of temazepam and diazepam. Her respiratory rate fell from 8 to 4 breaths per minute in the ambulance and she has now stopped breathing. Her pulse rate is 72 bpm and BP 104/64 mmHg. Her pupils are 4 mm and reactive. Her capillary glucose is 5.8 mmol/L.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of her respiratory arrest?
o: Upper airway obstruction by a foreign body
questions.e: Sedatives such as benzodiazepines depress the CNS and respiratory drive, causing respiratory arrest. Normal pupils make opioids less likely.

steps.x: This asks what is going on. Name the condition or finding from the stem before looking at the options.

clues: empty packets of temazepam and diazepam
fell from 8 to 4 breaths per minute
steps.x: Sedative overdose with slowly falling respiratory rate and normal pupils.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **CNS depression from benzodiazepines.**

elim: Sudden onset with focal signs; the empty packets explain this.
Her glucose is normal.
Gives pinpoint pupils; hers are normal size.
She is not choking; breathing slowed gradually.

steps.x: **B. CNS depression from benzodiazepines.** CNS depressants (opioids, sedatives, alcohol) are a key cause of respiratory arrest.

questions.stem: A 72 year old man with atrial fibrillation who is not anticoagulated suddenly develops vertigo, slurred speech and double vision. Thirty minutes later he becomes unresponsive and stops breathing. His pulse rate is 88 bpm and irregular, BP 196/104 mmHg. His capillary glucose is 7.2 mmol/L and his pupils are equal and normal size.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of his respiratory arrest?
questions.e: Vertigo, dysarthria and diplopia in a patient with untreated AF suggest posterior circulation (brainstem) stroke, which can abolish respiratory drive.

steps.x: This asks what is going on. Name the condition or finding from the stem before looking at the options.

clues: atrial fibrillation who is not anticoagulated
vertigo, slurred speech and double vision
steps.x: Embolic source + brainstem symptoms + then apnoea.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: The brainstem respiratory centre is hit: **brainstem stroke**.

elim: His glucose is normal.
No opioid history and normal pupils.
Causes hypotension and unilateral signs, not vertigo and diplopia.
Breathing continues and recovery is rapid.

steps.x: **A. Brainstem stroke.** Neurological causes of respiratory arrest: brainstem stroke, head injury.

questions.stem: A 19 year old woman with asthma has been wheezy for 2 days. In the Emergency Department she becomes exhausted and drowsy, then stops breathing. Her chest is not moving and she is centrally cyanosed. A carotid pulse is present at 52 bpm. Her oxygen saturation is 70% on 15 L/min oxygen via a non-rebreathe mask.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Severe asthma is a respiratory cause of respiratory arrest. No chest movement, cyanosis and a pulse still present define respiratory arrest; the bradycardia warns that cardiac arrest is near.

steps.x: This asks what is going on. Name the condition or finding from the stem before looking at the options.

clues: carotid pulse is present at 52 bpm
steps.x: Exhausted asthmatic, no chest movement, cyanosed, **pulse present** and slowing.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Respiratory arrest** from severe asthma.

elim: No allergen exposure, rash or angioedema; this is progressive asthma.
Her pulse is present.
She is cyanosed with no chest movement; this is real apnoea.
Breathing continues and she would recover quickly.

steps.x: **D. Respiratory arrest.** Severe asthma and COPD exacerbations can cause respiratory arrest.

questions.stem: A 68 year old man on a surgical ward is reviewed because the nurse cannot wake him. He has had regular oxycodone after a laparotomy. His respiratory rate is 2 breaths per minute with barely visible chest movement. His pulse rate is 60 bpm and BP 108/70 mmHg.
questions.q: Which other finding is most likely?
o: Central cyanosis with low oxygen saturation
questions.e: Respiratory arrest presents with apnoea or near apnoea, reduced chest movement, cyanosis, low oxygen saturation and altered GCS.

steps.x: This asks what is going on. Name the condition or finding from the stem before looking at the options.

clues: respiratory rate is 2 breaths per minute
steps.x: Opioid-depressed breathing almost stopped: **imminent respiratory arrest**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Not ventilating = **central cyanosis with low oxygen saturation**.

elim: He cannot be woken; GCS is reduced.
He is hypoventilating; pCO2 will be high.
Signs of an obstructed airway with strong effort; his drive is depressed.
Opioids cause pinpoint pupils.

steps.x: **A. Central cyanosis with low oxygen saturation.** Respiratory arrest signs: apnoea, reduced chest movement, cyanosis, low SpO2, altered GCS.

questions.stem: A 31 year old cyclist is hit by a car. At the scene he has a large scalp wound and a boggy swelling over the right temple. His GCS falls from 9 to 3 and he stops breathing. A carotid pulse is present at 54 bpm and BP is 186/100 mmHg. His right pupil is dilated and unreactive.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of his respiratory arrest?
questions.e: A falling GCS, blown pupil, hypertension and bradycardia (Cushing's response) show raised intracranial pressure after head injury, which can compress the brainstem and stop breathing.

steps.x: This asks what is going on. Name the condition or finding from the stem before looking at the options.

clues: boggy swelling over the right temple
right pupil is dilated and unreactive
steps.x: Head trauma + falling GCS + blown pupil + high BP and low pulse = **raised ICP**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Neurological cause: **severe head injury**.

elim: His BP is high, not low.
No opioid history and a unilateral dilated pupil.
No faint causes a fixed dilated pupil or apnoea.
Causes hypotension and tracheal deviation, not a blown pupil.

steps.x: **C. Severe head injury.** Head injury and trauma are causes of respiratory arrest.

questions.stem: An 84 year old woman with chronic kidney disease (eGFR 18 mL/min) was started on oral morphine for hip pain 4 days ago. She is now very drowsy and her respiratory rate is 5 breaths per minute. Her pulse rate is 62 bpm, BP 112/68 mmHg and oxygen saturation 84% breathing air. Her pupils are pinpoint.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of her reduced breathing?
questions.e: Morphine and its active metabolites are renally cleared, so they accumulate in CKD, causing mu-receptor respiratory depression with pinpoint pupils.

steps.x: This asks what is going on. Name the condition or finding from the stem before looking at the options.
Poor kidneys + new morphine + pinpoint pupils + slow breathing.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Opioid toxicity from renal impairment: **accumulation of morphine**.

elim: Causes confusion but not pinpoint pupils or a respiratory rate of 5.
Causes confusion and seizures, not pinpoint pupils.
Does not cause apnoea or pinpoint pupils.
Causes drowsiness, but the new opioid and pinpoint pupils point to drug toxicity.

steps.x: **A. Accumulation of morphine.** Opioids (including accumulation in CKD) cause respiratory depression with pinpoint pupils.

questions.stem: A 3 year old boy was eating peanuts when he suddenly coughed and gagged. He now cannot cry or cough, his lips are blue and he becomes unresponsive. He was well this morning with no fever. His pulse is present at 80 bpm.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of his respiratory arrest?
questions.e: Sudden choking while eating, then silent ineffective cough, cyanosis and unresponsiveness is complete airway obstruction by an inhaled foreign body.

steps.x: This asks what is going on. Name the condition or finding from the stem before looking at the options.
Sudden choke while eating, no illness = **airway obstruction**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Inhaled foreign body**.

elim: Comes on over hours with fever and drooling.
Gives rash, swelling and wheeze; the sudden choke while eating points to a foreign body.
A viral illness over days in infants.
Gives a barking cough and fever over days.

steps.x: **E. Inhaled foreign body.** Airway obstruction (choking, foreign body, tongue) causes respiratory arrest.

questions.stem: A 49 year old woman is intubated on the intensive care unit after a respiratory arrest. The tube is connected to waveform capnography. Over six ventilator breaths the capnography trace stays flat at zero. Her oxygen saturation is falling. Her pulse rate is 110 bpm and BP 128/80 mmHg, so she has a cardiac output.
questions.q: Which is the most likely explanation for the capnography trace?
questions.e: With a cardiac output present, no end-tidal CO2 at all means no gas is coming from ventilated lungs: the tube is in the oesophagus.

steps.x: This asks about a test. Decide what you need to find out, then pick the test or result that does it.
Circulation present but **no CO2** in exhaled gas.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: The tube is not in the lungs: **oesophageal intubation**.

elim: Gives a 'shark fin' sloping waveform, not a flat line.
Lowers end-tidal CO2 but a waveform is still present.
One lung is still ventilated, so CO2 is detected.
Does not abolish exhaled CO2.

steps.x: **C. Oesophageal intubation.** Flat capnography with a pulse = oesophageal tube. Capnography is the gold standard check.

questions.stem: A 57 year old man is intubated by the emergency team after a respiratory arrest on the ward. The registrar sees the chest rise and hears breath sounds on both sides. A colleague notices misting in the tube. The consultant wants the most reliable confirmation that the tube is in the trachea.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation?
questions.e: Waveform capnography is the gold standard for confirming tracheal tube placement; clinical signs such as chest rise, breath sounds and misting can all mislead.

steps.x: This asks about a test. Decide what you need to find out, then pick the test or result that does it.
Clinical signs are unreliable; you need an objective test.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Gold standard for tube position: **waveform capnography**.

elim: Supportive only; it can mislead.
Shows tube depth but not reliably trachea versus oesophagus, and is slow.
Can also occur with oesophageal placement.
Falls late after misplacement.

steps.x: **E. Waveform capnography.** Confirm every tracheal tube with waveform capnography.

questions.stem: A 33 year old man had a respiratory arrest from a methadone overdose. He was ventilated with a bag-valve mask for 10 minutes before he started breathing again. His respiratory rate is now 10 breaths per minute, pulse rate 96 bpm and oxygen saturation 90% on 15 L/min oxygen. An arterial blood gas is taken.
questions.q: Which is the most likely result?
o: Normal pH with low pCO2 and normal pO2
Respiratory acidosis with high pCO2 and low pO2
questions.e: Failure of ventilation causes hypoxaemia and hypercapnia, giving an acute respiratory acidosis. The ABG assesses both oxygenation and ventilation.

steps.x: This asks about a test. Decide what you need to find out, then pick the test or result that does it.

clues: respiratory arrest from a methadone overdose
steps.x: Under-ventilation: CO2 builds up, O2 falls.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Respiratory acidosis with high pCO2 and low pO2.**

elim: That fits vomiting with hyperventilation.
That fits compensated hyperventilation.
Hypoventilation does not cause alkalosis.
That fits hyperventilation, not apnoea.

steps.x: **C. Respiratory acidosis with high pCO2 and low pO2.** ABG after respiratory arrest: low pO2 (oxygenation) and high pCO2 (ventilation).

questions.stem: A 42 year old woman is found apnoeic at home and is ventilated by paramedics. She now breathes spontaneously but remains drowsy. Several empty unlabelled pill bottles were found beside her. Her pulse rate is 104 bpm, BP 108/66 mmHg and oxygen saturation 96% on oxygen. Her pupils are normal size.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation?
o: Paracetamol and salicylate levels with a toxicology screen
questions.e: When a drug overdose is suspected, bloods and a toxicology screen (including paracetamol and salicylate levels) identify the agent and treatable co-ingestions.

steps.x: This asks about a test. Decide what you need to find out, then pick the test or result that does it.
Apnoea from an unknown overdose.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Find the drugs: **paracetamol and salicylate levels with a toxicology screen**.

elim: No feature suggests PE.
Not the priority; she has an output and suspected overdose.
Not needed for drug-induced drowsiness.
No fever or meningism.

steps.x: **E. Paracetamol and salicylate levels with a toxicology screen.** Suspected overdose: bloods and toxicology screen, always with paracetamol levels.

questions.stem: A 79 year old man is found at the bottom of his stairs, apnoeic with a pulse. He is ventilated by bag-valve mask and later intubated. He takes apixaban. There is a large haematoma on his forehead. His pupils are unequal. His pulse rate is 56 bpm and BP 182/98 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation to identify the cause?
questions.e: Imaging is guided by the suspected cause: a fall on an anticoagulant with unequal pupils, bradycardia and hypertension suggests intracranial haemorrhage, so CT head is needed.

steps.x: This asks about a test. Decide what you need to find out, then pick the test or result that does it.
Fall on an anticoagulant with signs of raised ICP.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Image the suspected cause: **CT head**.

elim: Checks tube position but not the cause of the apnoea.
Not first-line in trauma with lateralising signs.
Slower and less practical in an unstable, intubated trauma patient.
Nothing suggests overdose; the cause is likely intracranial.

steps.x: **B. CT head.** After respiratory arrest, imaging is guided by the likely cause.

questions.stem: A 64 year old woman collapses in a restaurant. She is unresponsive with no chest movement but a carotid pulse is present. A doctor opens her airway with a head tilt-chin lift and sees a large piece of food lying at the back of her mouth.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
o: Blind finger sweep of the throat
questions.e: After opening the airway, remove any visible obstruction before inserting an adjunct or giving breaths. Blind finger sweeps are avoided.

steps.x: This asks what to do. Work out the clinical situation first, then the step that fits it.
Airway open, pulse present, obstruction **visible**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Remove the visible obstruction**, then ventilate.

elim: Can push the object further in; only remove what you can see and reach.
Airway adjuncts come after visible obstruction is removed.
Ventilation will not pass a visible obstruction; remove it first.
She has a pulse.

steps.x: **D. Remove the visible obstruction.** Respiratory arrest airway: open it, remove visible obstruction, adjunct, ventilate.

questions.stem: A 58 year old man is in the recovery room after a general anaesthetic for a hernia repair. He is unresponsive and not breathing despite a head tilt-chin lift. His chest is not moving. He does not gag when his mouth is examined. His pulse rate is 76 bpm and oxygen saturation 88%.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
questions.e: After general anaesthesia, loss of airway smooth muscle tone predisposes to obstruction; a simple adjunct such as an oropharyngeal airway, tolerated as he has no gag, keeps the airway open.

steps.x: This asks what to do. Work out the clinical situation first, then the step that fits it.
Post-anaesthetic airway obstruction, no gag reflex.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Simple adjunct: **insert an oropharyngeal airway**.

elim: No opioid features are given; the problem is loss of airway tone.
No signs of tension pneumothorax.
He has a pulse.
A last resort when all else fails.

steps.x: **A. Insert an oropharyngeal airway.** Post-GA airway obstruction: chin lift, then an oropharyngeal airway.

questions.stem: A 70 year old woman on a respiratory ward is found unresponsive. Her airway has been opened and an oropharyngeal airway inserted. She is still not breathing. A carotid pulse is present at 68 bpm. Her oxygen saturation is 79% and the crash team has been called.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
o: High-flow oxygen via a non-rebreathe mask
questions.e: With the airway open and an adjunct in place, an apnoeic patient with a pulse needs ventilation, best with a bag-valve mask and high-flow oxygen.

steps.x: This asks what to do. Work out the clinical situation first, then the step that fits it.
Airway sorted, still apnoeic, pulse present.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Breathe for her: **bag-valve-mask ventilation with high-flow oxygen**.

elim: She has a pulse, so compressions are not indicated.
Not indicated with a pulse.
She is not breathing, so a mask alone delivers nothing.
Only for patients who are breathing.

steps.x: **A. Bag-valve-mask ventilation with high-flow oxygen.** A non-rebreathe mask needs spontaneous breathing; apnoea needs ventilation.

questions.stem: A 35 year old man is brought in after injecting heroin. He is apnoeic with pinpoint pupils. His pulse rate is 60 bpm and BP 102/64 mmHg. His airway is open and he is being ventilated by bag-valve mask with high-flow oxygen. His oxygen saturation has risen to 92%.
questions.q: Which drug should be given alongside ventilatory support?
questions.e: If opioid overdose is the cause of respiratory arrest, give naloxone (an opioid antagonist) alongside ventilatory support.

steps.x: This asks what to do. Work out the clinical situation first, then the step that fits it.
Opioid respiratory arrest, already ventilated.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: The opioid antagonist: **naloxone**.

elim: Treats bradycardia, not opioid respiratory depression.
A respiratory stimulant not used for opioid overdose.
Reverses benzodiazepines, not opioids, and can cause seizures.
Treats paracetamol overdose.

steps.x: **E. Naloxone.** Opioid respiratory arrest: ventilate and give naloxone.

questions.stem: A 22 year old rugby player is tackled head first and lies motionless on the pitch. He has noisy, gurgling breathing that then stops. A carotid pulse is present at 90 bpm. He has no limb movement. The team doctor suspects a cervical spine injury and kneels at his head.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate way to open his airway?
o: Insert a laryngeal mask airway first
Log roll into the recovery position
questions.e: Head tilt-chin lift opens the airway, but jaw thrust is used when a cervical spine injury is suspected because it avoids neck extension.

steps.x: This asks what to do. Work out the clinical situation first, then the step that fits it.
Apnoea with a pulse and a possible neck injury.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Open the airway without moving the neck: **jaw thrust**.

elim: Extends the neck and risks worsening a cervical spine injury.
The airway must be opened manually first.
He is not breathing; open the airway first.
Moves the spine and does not open the airway.

steps.x: **C. Jaw thrust.** Head tilt-chin lift normally; jaw thrust if C-spine injury is a concern.

questions.stem: A 67 year old man is found slumped in his chair on a medical ward. He does not respond to voice or pain. A nurse opens his airway and looks, listens and feels for 10 seconds; he is not breathing. She is alone with him.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
o: Shout for help and check the carotid pulse
questions.e: Once he is found unresponsive and not breathing, call for help (the emergency team) and check circulation: a pulse means respiratory arrest needing ventilation; no pulse means CPR.

steps.x: This asks what to do. Work out the clinical situation first, then the step that fits it.

clues: does not respond to voice or pain
steps.x: Unresponsive and apnoeic: she needs help, and must know if there is a **pulse**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Shout for help and check the carotid pulse.**

elim: Help must be called first; you cannot run a resuscitation alone.
Not part of airway or breathing management.
Shout for help rather than leaving the patient.
Treat first; investigate once he is stabilised.

steps.x: **D. Shout for help and check the carotid pulse.** Respiratory arrest: airway, breathing, call for help, check pulse.

questions.stem: A 48 year old man who ate a large meal an hour ago is found apnoeic with a pulse after a fall. He is being ventilated with a bag-valve mask. The paramedic suggests inserting a laryngeal mask airway. His pulse rate is 72 bpm and oxygen saturation 90%.
questions.q: Which is the main risk of using a laryngeal mask airway in this patient?
questions.e: A laryngeal mask airway gives poor protection against gastric reflux, so it is unsuitable in a non-fasted patient; a cuffed tracheal tube protects the airway.

steps.x: This asks what to do. Work out the clinical situation first, then the step that fits it.

clues: ate a large meal an hour ago
steps.x: Full stomach + an airway that does not seal the trachea.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Aspiration of gastric contents.**

elim: An LMA sits above the cords and does not pass through them.
Possible but minor; not the main concern here.
Not a recognised complication of an LMA.
Only a tracheal tube can enter a bronchus.

steps.x: **A. Aspiration of gastric contents.** LMA = poor reflux protection; unsuitable if not fasted.

questions.stem: A 41 year old woman stops breathing after a large overdose of oxycodone. Ventilation is delayed. Her cardiac monitor shows sinus rhythm at 90 bpm, which slows over 6 minutes to 40 bpm and then to pulseless electrical activity. Her oxygen saturation is unrecordable.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of her slowing heart rate?
o: Hypoxaemia and hypercapnia causing myocardial hypoxia
questions.e: Untreated respiratory arrest causes progressive hypoxaemia and hypercapnia; myocardial hypoxia leads to bradyarrhythmias and then cardiac arrest.

steps.x: This asks about the mechanism. Connect the clinical picture to the physiology underneath it.
Apnoea, then slowing heart, then arrest.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Hypoxaemia and hypercapnia causing myocardial hypoxia.**

elim: Opioids are not directly cardiotoxic at this stage.
Takes hours and gives peaked T waves first.
She is unconscious and apnoeic.
Gives tachycardia and is not linked to the apnoea.

steps.x: **C. Hypoxaemia and hypercapnia causing myocardial hypoxia.** Respiratory arrest leads to cardiac arrest via hypoxic bradyarrhythmias.

questions.stem: A 7 month old girl with bronchiolitis becomes floppy and stops breathing on the paediatric ward. Her heart rate falls from 160 to 60 bpm over 2 minutes. She is ventilated with a bag-valve mask and her heart rate recovers to 150 bpm. A student asks how cardiac arrest usually happens in children.
questions.q: Which is the most common mechanism of cardiac arrest in children?
o: Respiratory arrest progressing to cardiac arrest
questions.e: In children, cardiac arrest is usually secondary: respiratory failure or arrest causes hypoxia, then bradycardia, then cardiac arrest (a respiratory-then-cardiac pattern).

steps.x: This asks about the mechanism. Connect the clinical picture to the physiology underneath it.
Breathing stopped first; the heart slowed; ventilation fixed it.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Respiratory arrest progressing to cardiac arrest.**

elim: Rare, and a cause of VF in young athletes.
A rare cause of arrhythmic arrest.
The commonest mechanism in adults with heart disease, not children.
An adult cause.

steps.x: **D. Respiratory arrest progressing to cardiac arrest.** Children arrest 'respiratory then cardiac'; that is why rescue breaths come first.

questions.stem: A 52 year old man is given repeated doses of IV morphine for renal colic. He becomes drowsy with a respiratory rate of 6 breaths per minute and pinpoint pupils. His oxygen saturation is 89% on 2 L/min oxygen. An arterial blood gas shows pH 7.24 and pCO2 9.1 kPa (4.7–6.0), yet his breathing does not speed up.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of his failure to respond to the high pCO2?
o: Mu-opioid receptor depression of the brainstem response to CO2
questions.e: Opioids agonise mu receptors in the brainstem respiratory centres, reducing the ventilatory response to hypercapnia, so breathing stays slow despite a high pCO2.

steps.x: This asks about the mechanism. Connect the clinical picture to the physiology underneath it.
High CO2 should drive breathing; with opioids it does not.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Mu-opioid receptor depression of the brainstem response to CO2.**

elim: Morphine does not paralyse the diaphragm.
That is the action of muscle relaxants.
Would increase breathing, not reduce it.
Would cause noisy breathing with effort, not a slow quiet rate.

steps.x: **B. Mu-opioid receptor depression of the brainstem response to CO2.** Opioids blunt the brainstem's response to CO2 via mu receptors.

questions.stem: A 45 year old woman is given propofol sedation for a dental procedure. She becomes unresponsive and starts snoring loudly, then her chest makes see-saw movements with no airflow. Her pulse rate is 82 bpm and oxygen saturation 86%. Lifting her chin restores airflow.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of her airway obstruction?
o: Loss of pharyngeal muscle tone under sedation
questions.e: Sedation and anaesthesia remove pharyngeal and laryngeal muscle tone, so the tongue and soft tissues fall back and obstruct the airway; chin lift or an adjunct relieves it.

steps.x: This asks about the mechanism. Connect the clinical picture to the physiology underneath it.
Effort but no airflow, fixed by chin lift = **soft tissue obstruction**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Loss of pharyngeal muscle tone under sedation.**

questions.stem: A 66 year old man was found apnoeic with a weak pulse after an overdose and was not ventilated for about 12 minutes. He was then resuscitated and his oxygen saturation is now 98%. Three days later he remains unresponsive with a GCS of 5 and myoclonic jerks. His sedation has been stopped.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of his brain injury?
questions.e: Prolonged respiratory arrest causes cerebral hypoxia, the major driver of brain injury when resuscitation is delayed.
